title: How to choose the right ETF for you
subtitle: Building a stock portfolio
openingQuestion: Two ETFs both track VN30, but ETF X has average daily trading volume of 2 million fund certificates, while ETF Y only has 20,000. What factor should make you think twice about ETF Y?
openingOptions: ETF Y must be charging a much higher management fee than ETF X
Nothing to worry about - same index means identical performance
Low liquidity makes it hard to buy/sell at a reasonable price
ETF Y will always return less than ETF X, on the same benchmark
explanation: Liquidity (trading volume) is one of the important criteria when choosing an ETF, even though it doesn't affect index-tracking performance. A low-liquidity ETF can have a wider bid-ask spread and be harder to match at a desired price, which is especially unfavorable when you need to sell urgently.

realWorldExample.company: Comparing domestic ETFs: E1VFVN30, FUEVFVND, FUESSVFL
realWorldExample.description: When choosing between ETFs tracking different index baskets in Vietnam, investors should compare not only the tracked asset (VN30 versus VNDiamond or VNFinlead) but also fund size (assets under management - AUM), daily trading liquidity, and expense ratio. An ETF with large AUM and high liquidity is usually more stable and easier to trade than a small, newly launched ETF.

quiz.question: When choosing an ETF, which of the following is NOT an important factor to consider?
options: Trading liquidity (average daily buy/sell volume)
Whether the asset/index tracked fits your investment goal
The color scheme of the fund manager's app interface
Expense ratio (annual management fee)
quiz.explanation: The core criteria for choosing an ETF are: cost (expense ratio), liquidity, fund size (AUM), and whether the tracked asset/index fits your risk appetite and goals. App interface design has nothing to do with the ETF's own quality.

quiz.question: Why does fund size (AUM - assets under management) matter when choosing an ETF?
options: Because AUM is the only metric you need to check when choosing a fund which is precisely why AUM belongs on the checklist
Because a larger AUM always means certainly higher investment returns
Because AUM directly affects how the benchmark index is calculated
Because too small an AUM risks the fund closing or merging
quiz.explanation: An ETF with too small an AUM (usually below a certain threshold) risks not being economically viable to sustain, leading to possible closure or merger - forcing the investor to receive cash back and find another fund, causing disruption and possibly unwanted tax/fee costs.

quiz.question: If your goal is long-term investment in Vietnam's stable large-cap stocks, which ETF among VN30, VNDiamond, or VNFinlead is the best fit to start with?
options: A VN30-tracking ETF - the broadest basket representing large caps
Choose VNFinlead because bank stocks always generate the highest returns
All three are the same, no need to consider any other factor
You should avoid ETFs entirely and buy individual stocks yourself for control
quiz.explanation: VN30 broadly represents 30 large-cap stocks across many different sectors, giving better diversification than sector-specific ETFs like VNFinlead (focused only on finance). For a beginner wanting a stable portfolio foundation, a broad-index ETF like VN30 is usually a more sensible starting choice.

quiz.question: Two ETFs both track VN30, one charging 0.6%/year, the other 0.2%/year. After 20 years, how does that fee difference matter?
options: Not significant since 0.4% is too small a number compared to market volatility
It erodes accumulated return since fees compound yearly
It only matters in the first year, after which a larger fund naturally lowers fees
It's offset by the higher-fee fund since they pick better stocks within the basket
quiz.explanation: The management fee is deducted from assets every year, so the deducted portion also loses its ability to compound in the years after. With the same benchmark index, the lower-fee ETF almost always ends up ahead - and a passive ETF doesn't 'pick better stocks', both simply replicate the exact VN30 basket.

quiz.question: What does an ETF's tracking error measure?
options: The margin of error when the fund manager publishes end-of-day net asset value
The gap between the buying price and selling price on the exchange at a point in time
The gap between the fund's performance and the performance of the index it tracks
The volatility of the benchmark index compared to its multi-year average
quiz.explanation: Tracking error is the deviation between an ETF's return and the return of the index it replicates, arising from fees, undeployed cash, and portfolio-rebalancing timing. The gap between buy and sell price is the bid-ask spread, a different concept about liquidity.

keyTakeaways: Four core criteria for choosing an ETF: management fee (expense ratio), trading liquidity, fund size (AUM), and whether the tracked asset/index fits your investment goal
Low liquidity can make it hard to buy/sell at a reasonable price, especially unfavorable when you need to trade urgently or in large volume
A broad-index ETF (like VN30) is usually more suitable as a portfolio foundation for beginners than a narrow sector-specific ETF

practicePrompt.question: You're deciding between 2 ETFs: ETF P (AUM VND 5,000 billion, fee 0.7%/year, high trading volume) and ETF Q (AUM VND 50 billion, fee 0.5%/year, very low trading volume). You plan to invest VND 500 million long-term. What should you prioritize?
options: Weigh all 4 criteria instead of just choosing the lowest fee, since low AUM creates risk when selling
Always choose the ETF with the lowest management fee, since this is the only factor that truly affects long-term investment results
Always choose the ETF with the largest AUM in the market, regardless of whether the benchmark index fits your investment goal
There's no meaningful difference between the two funds, since both are commonly called ETF fund certificates on the exchange
practicePrompt.explanation: The four criteria (fee, liquidity, AUM, tracked index) need to be weighed together - ETF Q's lower fee doesn't offset the liquidity risk when you need to trade a large volume.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Score an ETF
application.message: The lesson already has a real example scoring E1VFVN30 against the 4 criteria - see the 'Real example' section above. Now pick another ETF trading in Vietnam and score it yourself using those same 4 criteria.
application.secondary: Getting used to checking these four criteria will help you choose ETFs faster and more confidently.

sections.text: After understanding what an ETF is, the natural next question is: there are so many ETFs, which one should I choose? This is where you need a clear set of criteria instead of picking randomly by a familiar-sounding name.
Criterion 1: Does the tracked asset/index fit your goal

First, determine which basket of assets that ETF tracks. In Vietnam there are popular options like VN30 (the 30 largest-cap stocks, multi-sector), VNDiamond (large-cap stocks that have hit their foreign-ownership limit, attractive to foreign investors who can't buy directly), VNFinlead (focused on financial-sector stocks - banking). If you want a balanced, multi-sector portfolio, a VN30-tracking ETF is usually a more sensible foundation than narrow sector-specific ETFs.

As mentioned in the previous lesson, even a small management cost accumulates meaningfully over a long horizon. When comparing two ETFs tracking the same index, prioritize the one with a lower expense ratio, since index-tracking performance is essentially the same.

Liquidity is measured by average daily trading volume. A high-liquidity ETF lets you buy/sell easily near net asset value (NAV), while a low-liquidity ETF may have a wider bid-ask spread, meaning you might pay more to buy or receive less when selling than the actual value.

items: Tracked asset/index: does it match your goal and risk appetite
Expense ratio: annual management fee, the lower the better if other factors are equal
Liquidity: average daily trading volume, affecting your ability to buy/sell at a reasonable price
Fund size (AUM): too small a fund risks closure or merger, disrupting the investor

sections.label: Criterion 4: Fund size (AUM)
sections.text: AUM (Assets Under Management) is the total value of assets a fund manages. An ETF with too small an AUM may not be economically viable to sustain long-term, leading to a risk of closure or merger into another fund. In that case, the investor is forced to take back cash and find a replacement fund - disrupting long-term investment plans, and possibly triggering unwanted tax or trading costs.

A simple approach for beginners: start with a broad-index ETF, with large AUM, high liquidity and low fees (for example a VN30-tracking ETF from a reputable, long-established fund manager), then once you've gained experience and better understand your own risk appetite, consider adding sector- or theme-specific ETFs to further diversify your portfolio.
A real example: scoring E1VFVN30 on the 4 criteria

items: Management fee: 0.65%/year - among the lowest of the domestic ETFs
Total expense ratio: about 0.9%/year - the figure to use for comparing ETFs, not just the management fee alone
Tracked index: VN30 - the 30 largest-cap stocks on HOSE
Rebalancing frequency: every 6 months (January and July), matching HOSE's schedule for reviewing the VN30 basket

sections.label: How to apply this to another ETF
sections.text: Use these same 4 criteria (plus average trading volume and fund AUM if available) to score any other ETF trading in Vietnam, then compare against E1VFVN30 as a benchmark.

lines: Choosing an ETF shouldn't be based on a familiar name but on four criteria: tracked asset, cost, liquidity, and fund size.
For beginners, a broad-index ETF with large AUM, high liquidity, and low fees is usually the safest starting point.
